Make your site agent-ready

A 15-point checklist for websites that people and AI agents can both use.

All items

Showing 15 of 15

  • Structure

    Agents and screen readers both navigate by landmarks and headings. A page without them is a wall of divs.

    How: Use header, nav, main and footer. One h1, then h2 and h3 without skipping levels.

  • Structure

    A div with a click handler has no role, no name and no keyboard path, so an agent cannot tell it is interactive.

    How: Use button for actions and a with href for navigation. Never attach onClick to a div or span.

  • Structure

    Agents locate controls by their accessible name. Icon-only buttons and generated class names give them nothing to hold on to.

    How: Give every control visible text or an aria-label. Keep names stable across releases.

  • Structure

    Many agents fetch HTML once. Content that only appears after a script runs is invisible to them.

    How: Render the main content as HTML. Use scripts to enhance, not to reveal.

  • Content

    Idioms, puns and marketing fog read as noise to a parser and to a tired reader alike.

    How: Say what the thing is and what happens next. Delete words that do no work.

  • Content

    If the menu says Archive and the toast says Moved to storage, an agent cannot tell they are the same action.

    How: Pick one word for each action and object. Use it everywhere, including errors and docs.

  • Content

    An agent, like a screen-reader user, often sees only the list of links. "Click here" says nothing.

    How: Write "Read the pricing page", not "Learn more". Make every link text unique on the page.

  • Actions

    A placeholder vanishes on input. Without a label an agent must guess what the field wants.

    How: Use label with for, plus autocomplete, type and inputmode so the field states its format.

  • Actions

    If a submit changes nothing visible, an agent cannot know whether it worked, and may retry.

    How: Show a status message in a live region, or navigate to a confirmation page with a clear heading.

  • Actions

    "Something went wrong" gives neither a person nor an agent a next step.

    How: Write the fix as an instruction, mark the field aria-invalid and point aria-describedby at the message.

  • Actions

    An agent acting on your behalf should not be able to delete something with a single ambiguous click.

    How: Repeat the consequence in the confirm button, or offer an undo that stays until dismissed.

  • Data

    Prices, opening hours and product details are easier to read as data than to infer from layout.

    How: Add JSON-LD for the page type. Keep it in sync with the visible text.

  • Data

    The first thing an agent reads about a page is its head. A missing description means a guessed summary.

    How: Set a title, a meta description, og:title, og:description and og:image with alt text.

  • Trust

    Agents check what they may read. Ambiguous rules lead to over-blocking or over-fetching.

    How: Publish robots.txt and a sitemap. Say explicitly which paths automated readers may use.

  • Trust

    An agent that hits an unexplained 429 cannot adapt. A documented limit lets it back off correctly.

    How: Document rate limits and return Retry-After. Give a contact address for automated-access questions.

Five things an agent needs

Each checklist item belongs to one of these. Every one of them also helps a person using a screen reader, a slow connection or a small screen.

    Markup an agent can walk without guessing.

    4 items

  • Content

    Words that mean one thing, to a person or a parser.

    3 items

  • Actions

    Forms and buttons that state what they do and report what happened.

    4 items

  • Data

    Facts the agent can read directly instead of scraping.

    2 items

  • Trust

    Clear limits, so automation knows where it may act.

    2 items

About this checklist

What it is. Agent Ready is a short, opinionated list of things a website needs so that an AI agent acting for a person, such as a shopping assistant or a research tool, can read it and act on it without guessing. Most items are plain web fundamentals.

How the score works. Every item counts once. The score is the share of items you have ticked. It is a self-assessment, not an audit: ticking an item records your judgment, nothing is scanned.

Where your progress lives. Ticks and the site name are saved in this browser only, using local storage. Nothing is sent anywhere. Use Download report to keep a copy or share it with your team.
